#8153. The Awkward Truth About Gym Class

Pretend you’re a tree. This was my earliest memory of physical education: our teacher, a tall and thin woman whose broad nimbus of dark hair was edged with gray, asking us to make-believe. By, as I understood it, not moving. In gym class. I was in second grade, and I was already confused. Somewhere here in my elementary school’s wood-floored gymnasium, I knew, there were ropes to climb, mats to tumble on, balls to kick and throw and dodge. And yet we were being corralled into this dumbed-down modern dance — the kind of hippie sh*t, I would later understand, that was typical of our Western Massachusetts college town.

Not that I was craving, or ever did crave, a traditional gym class. I was not made for gym. I was small — perpetually the second shortest boy in my grade — and slight and uninterested in the big sports that make up the bulk of public-school gym. I did not own a catcher’s mitt; no sane, responsible adult would let this shrimp play football.

At the same time, I was physical. I was a kid, after all. I wanted to run around, try a handstand, lift a dumbbell, shoot a basket, make a goal. And as uncoordinated and unenthusiastic as I was, I was not entirely untalented. I remember running a seven-minute mile in fourth grade. I could touch my toes and put one foot behind my head. My friend Jason and I competed to see who would be the first to knock out 60 sit-ups in a minute. I don’t remember who won.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class.

Those achievements and activities, however, had nothing to do with gym class as I experienced it. In the same way that English class was not designed to make philistines love literature, or biology to inspire dedication to the scientific method, gym class was not about converting us into athletes. Instead, it was a class for the kids who already were athletes, who played baseball and field hockey for fun, who owned weight machines at home, who didn’t need to sit through the gym teacher’s confounding explanation of what it meant to be “offsides.” I didn’t begrudge them their special class. I could spell and do algebra. They could throw an arcing spiral. This was the way of the world, even in a Massachusetts town full of ex-hippies.

And that all would have been just fine — if gym class had stuck with the most mainstream of sports. I could suck at soccer and blow at basketball, because who cared? Instead, gym class branched out, and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Swimming was a particular source of trauma. When I was 8, during a year my family spent living in Brighton, England, I was so tearfully reluctant to get in the pool that the headmaster of the school had to personally throw me in. And as I got older, the trauma morphed: Back in Massachusetts, the locker room after eighth-grade swimming lessons was a horror movie — I, the underdeveloped shrimp, had to undress surrounded by my Sasquatchian contemporaries. I have a memory of once changing entirely inside a locker, but that can’t be real. Those things were barely 10 inches wide. But another memory is definitely real: During one class, I dived into the deep end — and the force of the water as I entered yanked my swimsuit to my ankles. I don’t know how I had the wherewithal to pull them up before surfacing, but I did. I guess I was learning something.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class. Already awkward around girls, not to mention the implied romance of ballroom dance, I had the misfortune to be paired with Turtle Butt. Who was Turtle Butt? I don’t know. She was a girl I’d never spoken to, but one of my good friends had decided to call her Turtle Butt, even though, as far as I could tell, her butt did not resemble a turtle. And I was going to have to dance with her! Oh, the humiliation!

Gym class has always branched out from mainstream sports — and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Nearly 40 years later, I can now acknowledge that the humiliation was solely in my own head. I remember the potential embarrassment with infinitely more clarity than I remember any actual jeers or taunts, because there were none. But such is the world of the adolescent, where fears and anxieties dwarf reality.

And what I feared most of all was being seen. In other classes this didn’t happen. You might know where the Mason-Dixon Line was — or not. You might know how to deploy the quadratic formula — or not. Either way, you were not exposing anything about yourself other than your intellectual ability, or lack thereof.

It was similar in gym class. We all knew that some kids had it and some didn’t, and there was no shame in being terrible. (Asthma reduced my mile time to 20 minutes by eighth grade. But so what?) The difference, however, was that in gym class, unlike in history or math, you were a physical being. Strip away your ability to perform, and there you still stood, surrounded by your classmates, in sneakers and sweats or the jeans and T-shirt you wore to school that morning. You could pretend you’re a tree all you want — you remained visible: your prepubescent stature, your hairless lack of muscle tone, your terrapin posterior. There were no desks to hide behind, no escape from their eyes and their judgment.

No escape — except, perhaps, to grow up a little. In high school, my family moved to Southeastern Virginia, a place you’d think would have a sports and gym-class culture more extreme than that of the academic Yankees. Instead, gym was even more of an afterthought, not even required after sophomore or maybe junior year. Just like in second grade, I was confused. The school was full of jocks — guys who played soccer and football, girls on the field hockey team — and yet gym class was lackadaisical at best. Driver’s ed occupied a couple of months of the curriculum, and on Fridays, we’d ride a school bus to a nearby bowling alley, where nerds like me, who had no hope of throwing a strike, could at least show off by knowing how to score the game correctly.

Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not.

In fact, I considered the bowling alley my place — because I was there all the time, after school. Technically, not in the bowling alley, but just outside, where almost every day I would meet my skateboarder friends to ride the concrete drainage ditch next to its parking lot. In high school, skating had become my life, my all-consuming hobby, my… my… sport? Yes, my sport! After having failed at all of the mainstream sports, I’d finally found this one sweaty, filthy, wonderful way to be an athlete (though I would never have used that word back then). And while I wasn’t pro material, I wasn’t too bad at it, either. I could hold my own among my friends, at competitions in Virginia Beach, on road trips to Richmond and Washington, D.C. And more important, I could do so without fretting about being seen, in some unspeakable way, by the kids around me. Skateboarding required us to accept one another, in all our foibles and weirdnesses. Because if we didn’t, then who would we skate with?

I stuck with skateboarding for most of a decade, before aging out postcollege and taking up distance running and, more recently, rock climbing. As with skateboarding, I’m pretty good at both, if not truly exceptional, and I appreciate the physical experience of each in ways I could not have imagined in high school. At times, I’ve wondered: If gym class had taught us how to run, or how to scale a boulder, would I have discovered and loved those sports decades earlier? Somehow, I doubt it. Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not. What mattered was what happened after school, in every sense of the term. Still, gym class did teach me this one important lesson about public education: If you make like a tree, you can leave.

#8151. The Unexpected Gift That Everyone Will Be Fighting Over At Your Holiday White Elephant

Turns out, the most steal-worthy gift might also be the most practical.

White Elephant gifts fall into two categories. There’s the novelty item that gets a huge laugh, takes one triumphant lap around the room, and disappears into the black hole at the back of your closet. Then there’s the unexpected G.O.A.T everyone clamors for. It’s useful. It’s clever. It leaves everyone thinking “Why didn’t I think of that?”

This year, we’re making a case for a sleeper hit: a pack of Energizer® Ultimate Lithium® AA batteries. Hear us out.

Sure, batteries might not spark the immediate razzle-dazzle of a mini karaoke machine or a candle shaped like a plate of spaghetti. But they do have something arguably more powerful: the ability to solve a future problem. These pocket-sized powerhouses keep your life going. Especially when we’re talking about the holidays.

Picture it. It’s December. The house is lit up like a regional airport runway. Your kid has acquired approximately 11 new objects that beep, flash, sing, or inexplicably do all three. Somewhere in your home, a tiny screwdriver is about to become the most important object you own.

In the midst of all this, the question hits you. Did you remember to buy batteries? Exactly. Why should you stock up on Energizer® batteries for this year’s white elephant? Let us count the ways.

There’s something deeply satisfying about having an aggressively stocked battery drawer. It’s the domestic equivalent of having a full tank of gas and remembering to defrost the chicken before 5 p.m.

Energizer® Ultimate Lithium® AA batteries have a 25 year shelf life, which means your White Elephant contribution could conceivably still be hanging around when today’s toddlers are complaining about their own toddlers.

That also makes them the rare holiday gift that comes with absolutely no urgency. Nobody needs to exchange them for another size. Nobody has to smile politely while wondering whether the gift giver simply regifted the item. Nobody needs to dig it out of the back of the dresser to wear the one time the gifter comes by a year.

They call it the battery drawer for a reason. And one day, perhaps years from now, you open it in a moment of need and discover them sitting there. Cause you planned ahead.

December has a way of revealing just how much of your home is quietly powered by AA batteries.

The flameless candles? Batteries. The light-up garland? Batteries. The singing stuffed reindeer Grandma bought your child despite your explicit request for “nothing with sounds”? You better believe that thing needs batteries.

Just when you thought you were out of the woods, Christmas morning arrives and ushers in a fresh crop of tiny battery-powered overlords. Race cars. Remote controls. Games. Noise-making toys that leave you wondering whether the toy’s product designer has ever met a parent.

Energizer® Ultimate Lithium® is the #1 longest-lasting AA battery, designed to keep the devices your family relies on going and going.

Is it slightly ironic to give someone batteries that could keep their kid’s noisiest toy going and going? Yes. That’s the risk you take.

So batteries? Batteries are getting forgotten.

They are perhaps the quintessential “Oh, shoot!” holiday purchase. The thing you realize you need precisely when every store is closed, and a child is staring at you with the devastated expression of someone whose brand-new toy is apparently just a decorative object now.

Which is why Energizer® Ultimate Lithium® AA batteries make such a sneaky-good White Elephant gift. You’re not really giving someone batteries. You’re giving them the ability to skip one future panic trip to the store.

So yes, wrap up the batteries. Everyone can laugh when they’re opened. Until the snatching starts.

#8149. 10 Great Sports Docs & True-Life Stories To Stream With Your Kids Right Now

From inspiring stories to crucial moments in history to cutting edge contermporary atheletes, there’s a great co-viewing experience for everyone.

Finding movies and TV that please everyone can be tough. But if you’ve got a sporty kid, screen time is a great opportunity. Sure, there’s old-school sports movie like The Sandlot or A League of Their Own — complete with inspirational messages and strong moral codes. But why go for fictional sports stories when you can get the real thing?

Sports docuseries, or true-to-life dramatized sports stories, are great to watch with young athletes. They tell inspirational tales and maybe even give them a real-life role model in the meantime. From a variety of different sports to a selection of different formats, we’ve thought about the watchability and the relevance of each of these selections. There should be something for everyone in this list. And, at the very least, with each, you and your kid will learn something.

This documentary film focuses on several different Paralympic athletes, all of whom have truly amazing stories. Warning for parents: This documentary is not for the faint of heart, as some of the physical challenges are truly harrowing. For example, Bebe Vio — who inspired the name of the documentary — lost all of her limbs to meningitis at the age of 11. She nonetheless went on to become a wheelchair fencer. Deeply inspiring, this doc is great for teens interested in sports and perhaps great for all of us to have a little perspective on the amazing nature of the human spirit.

The 2004 story of the Boston Red Sox is a great one in terms of an underdog story. Even if you’re not a Red Sox fan, this story represents a very specific time in baseball and tells the story of how this iconic team broke a curse that had existed since 1918. If your kid is just starting to get into baseball, this documentary series might seem like ancient history; after all, 2004 was more than 20 years ago. And yet, this particular season for many of us feels very recent and still relevant.

Who doesn’t love trick shots? This 30 for 30 ESPN doc is all about a group of five guys who were former college roommates who created a sports comedy entertainment phenomenon. Focused on trick shots and betting, this doc is 100% for older kids. But if you’ve got a teen who is into sports and loves to joke around, this is a great, quirky documentary focused on male friendship, humor, and creating something nobody has ever done before.

Everybody is obsessed with Travis Kelce, but his brother Jason Kelce might be the more interesting of the siblings, at least as an athlete. The 2023 documentary film chronicles the 2022 Philadelphia Eagles season, with a specific focus on Kelce. The main tension here is whether or not Kelce will retire from the NFL. Weird topic for kids? Well, for tweens and teens interested in unpacking the real-deal toll of being in the NFL, there’s something smartly educational about this. You may be young and obsessed with football now, but life is long.

Not technically a documentary, this is a docudrama based on the true story of Ray McElrathbey, who deals with a ton of family adversity and racism. Set in the early 2000s, McElrathbey’s story is inspiring and very family-oriented. Again, this one might be for older kids, but the script is from Nick Santora of Reacher and Sopranos fame, so there’s a breezy and very focused feeling to this movie.

Here’s another docudrama that is based on a real-life movement in India, centered on teenagers and skateboarding culture. In the film, a young girl named Prerna (Rachel Sanchita Gupta) finds purpose and belonging through skateboarding. The film is a heartwarming coming-of-age movie, but watching it with your kid means you’re also giving them a dose of contemporary history. The production for the film also worked very closely with rural villages in India to make sure it accurately portrayed the culture and struggles of teenagers.

A great one to watch with your aspiring skateboarding kid, or maybe a kid who isn’t sure what their athletic interest might be.

One of the greatest athletes of our time is also the subject of a one-of-a-kind docuseries. Released in 2024, Simone Biles Rising is all about the gymnast’s comeback. The fact that Biles has been so transparent about her mental health has been a groundbreaking part of the conversations about young athletes. As both a role model and someone who is part of living history, Biles is a figure that should inspire conversation with your curious athlete.

This 10-part documentary changed everything back in 2020. However, at this point, The Last Dance — which tells the story of one of the greatest periods of the Chicago Bulls — almost feels vintage. Chances are, for certain parents, you didn’t have a kid old enough to watch this documentary nearly seven years ago. And, if you’re of the generation that lived through the Bulls’ 1990s dynasty, then you owe it to share that history with your kid.

Not everything about Michael Jordan and his teammates is admirable, to be clear. But the thing about some great sports history is that it can be messy.

Focused on the 2024 X Games, The Rise: Gold Medal Girls of the X Games focuses on four teen athletes, Arisa Trew, Shiloh Catori, Reese Nelson, and Jada Ward. Those are all skateboarders, and that’s just the most recent season. More broadly, The Rise covers all sorts of women’s sports, from skating to the WNBA. If you have a young woman looking for some new role models, you can’t miss with the various seasons of The Rise.

You can really start anywhere with this excellent docuseries. But the most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained is focused on the 2024 Tour de France. Obviously, the famous bicycle race has existed since 1903, but it’s really only recently that we could actually document this incredible event. Even the least sporty kid in the world can get excited about people using their bodies to propel a bicycle forward. And the most sporty kids will have trouble wrapping their mind around the sheer effort it takes to traverse 2,200 miles over 24 days over some of the hilliest terrain on Earth.

The most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained, released in 2025, is now the last season of this docuseries. The real Tour de France hasn’t gone anywhere, of course. In fact, it’s happening right now. Meaning if you get your kid excited enough, you can watch the 2026 Tour de France as it’s happening. Or watch a little contemporary Tour de France, then go back and watch Unchained on Netflix.

#8146. 32 Gifts For The Mom Who Has One Good Outfit & Wears It Everywhere

No wardrobe overhaul needed, just a few clever pieces to make her feel more put together.

Listen. Moms are juggling about a million things every minute of every day. We're bopping all over the place, half-frantic half the time, scooting kids from school to extracurriculars and keeping everyone's schedules from imploding and, and, and... the list is literally never-ending. So, yeah, maybe we reach for the same outfit or some spin on it every time we leave the house. Our unofficial uniform most days is black yoga pants and an oversized sweatshirt. And, sure, there are many days when we look like Adam Sandler's stunt double rolling through the school pickup line. Hey, whatever; it works. It's comfy and reliable.

That doesn't mean that even the most prolific outfit repeater hasn't caught a stray glimpse of herself in the mirror and thought, Hmm, my wardrobe could use a little love. Enter: these gifts. Trust, we're not here to talk anyone out of their uniform. (Respectfully, we would never.) We’re just talking about giving her a few pieces that will make her feel fresh and more put-together on the days she wants to try something different. A statement boot, a chic pullover, a bandana for a pop of print, jewelry she’ll never take off: small swaps that turn “I just threw this on” into “This is exactly the look I was going for” without a ton of effort or extra thought.

Our editors rounded up the pieces that have been reviving our go-to outfits — and confidence — lately.

This bracelet has become one of my most-worn pieces! The Nigella is a delicate, stacked look that hits that perfect sweet spot between casual enough to wear every day and special enough to feel like real jewelry. It’s the kind of gift that comes in a beautiful box, looks significantly more expensive than it is, and immediately becomes a daily staple for whoever is lucky enough to receive it. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social

I’ve heard nothing but rave reviews about Rothy’s for years, but I’d never owned a pair myself. This now marks my second pair, and I wish I’d started buying them sooner. A bold shoe is such an easy way to switch up your same old outfits, and these Ivy Sneakers make a statement without trying too hard. The dark cheetah print has a soft, suede-like finish; they come with an extra pair of bright red laces for a pop of color; and they’re seriously comfy. Oh, and I LOVE that they’re knit from recycled plastic bottles! — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

This is the year I got into bandanas, and I own a few Handker brand ones that have held up so well. They add a small (so not overwhelming for us black wearers) pop of color and a print, and you can wear them in so many styles on your neck alone. But they also look great in your hair, tied to a belt loop, or on your bag. They're a super affordable way to play with color and pattern, and jazz up the pieces you already own and love to wear. — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

I feel way cooler than I actually am every single time I put on this jacket. Between its vintage bomber energy, fun California-inspired patches, and slightly oversized fit, it adds personality to anything you pair it with. I chose the plum color, which is literal perfection for fall and winter, and it looks equally stunning with or without the removable faux-fur collar. Also, if you’re unsure what to wear with it, Carve Designs offers outfit suggestions on their site. — Julie Sprankles

When I hear anything called "viral" I usually get suspicious, but after I tried these lovely plastic-free solid lip serums, I was a convert. These look so nice and keep your lips smooth forever — usually you either get color or a lip treatment, but this feels like it does both equally well. And the packaging just feels special. These are three new Mexican dessert flavors/shades, and they are my new favorites. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social

Say you're a Swiftie and love the song "The Fate of Ophelia." Or say you just really love kickass women and want to reclaim that. Then Hysteria is the brand for you. These pieces are ornate and pretty and make just about any outfit. This Ophelia necklace in particular is a showstopper. — Kate Auletta, Editor-in-Chief

This is the bag for the mom who found one outfit that works and has been wearing it on rotation since 2019. The Petal Parade Crossbody is the kind of accessory that makes a simple jeans-and-top combo look completely intentional and pulled together without requiring a single additional effort, and the floral beaded design is vibrant, joyful, and genuinely eye-catching in a way that reads as stylish rather than trying too hard. This ear cuff is SO pretty! It’s crystal-encrusted and sparkly, and it just instantly elevates any outfit. I really appreciate the fact that it doesn’t require a new piercing, too. It comes in a few other fun colorways, and I’ve already got my eye on a few so I can create a sparkly little stack. — Julie Sprankles

What do you need to go with your one good outfit? How about your one perfect winter coat? This coat makes me feel so special and put together. For the mom who has one good outfit and wears it everywhere, the right sneaker is the whole foundation and these are genuinely it. My kids are both teens now, and I swear I get more sentimental with every passing year. This moto jacket is my secret cheat code for looking put-together in two seconds flat. First of all, the vegan leather feels amazingly soft and luxe. I’ve long believed that a good pair of boots can make any woman feel like a total put-together badass, but I’m over 40 now... boots can’t just be aesthetic; they also have to be comfortable. This necklace has become one of my most-worn pieces! One of my favorite outfit hacks is wearing something really simple, like a white T-shirt and jeans with a really fun pair of sneakers. Enter these fun sneakers. #8143. The 2-Minute Lard Trick That Helps Smaller Songbirds Get Their Fair Share of Food in Fall and Winter

Smearing fat onto tree bark mimics natural foraging to help smaller nuthatches, wrens, and chickadees feast safely while keeping bully-boy starlings at bay.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you're feeding garden birds this fall, you'll know that fat balls and suet feeders are often mobbed by dominant birds like starlings and grackles, leaving nothing for more timid feathered friends to feast upon – which is why you should also smear a little lard on a tree or fencepost. Adding fat to your bird feeding buffet is essential as temperatures fall, but small birds who need this energy-boost most often miss out. However, this quick bird-feeding trick ensures smaller, shyer nuthatches, chickadees, titmice, wrens and creepers get their fair share of high-energy fuel, because bigger birds are unable to cling to this vertical surface to feed.

Smearing lard, tallow or vegetable shortening onto a tree only takes two minutes4 but this simple addition really can make a difference to how smaller garden songbirds fare in winter. The smaller a bird is, the more vulnerable it is to freezing or starving as temperatures drop, and the more likely it is to be bullied from feeders by more aggressive birds. This fat-smear trick bypasses those bullying birds, mimicking natural foraging to tempt even cautious birds like brown creepers who are far too shy to use regular feeders.

If you like to feed birds in winter, tree-smeared lard can attract unusual visitors like woodpeckers to your yard as insects become scarce, and you'll also enjoy watching nuthatches walk headfirst down the tree trunk to enjoy their fat feast. Smearing lard on a tree also avoids the danger of smaller birds getting their tongues, claws or legs tangled in a fat-ball mesh holder. You can also easily mix birdseed into the fat to provide extra nutrients, or try our super-tasty bark butter recipe below.

Any tree or fencepost will do, but aim for a more mature tree or older fencepost that has furrows or cracks that will hold more lard and give clinging birds a foothold. Take a golf-ball sized chunk of lard, tallow or vegetable shortening and press it onto the wood, ideally 5-6 feet high, on the shady side of the tree or post so it doesn’t melt in the sun.

Mix in a pinch of cayenne pepper to deter squirrels if needs be, as they’ll quickly learn to leave it alone while birds are unaffected by the taste and heat. Only smear enough fat on the tree for birds to finish during daylight hours to avoid attracting nocturnal scavengers like racoons and opossums. And if you live in bear country, wait until late November or December when they're in full hibernation before trying this trick.

You can use animal-based lard or tallow, and plant-based vegetable shortening to feed garden birds in winter using this quick trick.

Lard is cheap, full of fast energy for birds and has a soft, buttery texture so is easily pressed into bark furrows. Look for a product that’s 100% pure lard such as South Chicago Packing Lard, available from Amazon. You’ll find similar products at most grocery stores but read the ingredients list carefully: while you don’t need to worry about citric acid, avoid synthetic stabilizers like propyl gallate, BHT or BHA, commonly added to grocery-store lard to prevent it going rancid. Don't use products with added salt or sodium as birds can't process it and high levels can be fatal.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Tallow is simply suet in rendered form and, again, you need to look for a product that’s 100% tallow such as Farmer Bob’s 100% Beef Tallow, available from Amazon. It has a similar consistency to lard and has a higher nutritional value as well as being a great source of energy.

Vegetable shortening is less nutritious but it still provides a valuable high-energy boost to small songbirds in cold conditions. For regular use, an organic all-vegetable shortening such as Spectrum Naturals Organic Shortening, available from Walmart is best. Unrefined and free of synthetic preservatives, it retains some nutrients and is firm enough to use for this trick. It's fine to use Crisco, also available from Walmart, if that’s what you already have in your panty, but it’s less nutritious and melts more easily so think of it as an occasional junk-food treat for birds.

In the North, Midwest and Mountain West, temperatures are cold enough to simply smear lard or tallow straight onto the tree or post without it melting or spoiling in fall and winter. Vegetable shortening will need mixing with cornmeal to stiffen it up before using. Of course, you can still add ingredients to lard and tallow to increase the nutritional value.

In the South and Southwest, mild fall and winter days can be warm enough to soften lard, tallow and vegetable shortening, so mix with cornmeal to form a firmer dough before using.

While plain lard smeared onto a tree or fencepost works just fine, this no-cook recipe will tempt even the shyest feeders. Mixing a handful of natural, raw ingredients into the fat also creates a pliable dough that’s the perfect consistency to press into bark furrows in all zones.

Providing food for small, shy songbirds in this way is a useful part of a bird-food buffet in fall and winter. The more ways you can offer food, the better, from planting berried shrubs that provide a natural feast for winter birds to saving kitchen scraps for your feathered friends. Different species prefer different food types and also to feed in various ways, so using a range of bird feeders to satisfy different species is a smart move, too. Just don't forget to cater for the smallest backyard birds with this quick lard-smear trick.

#8142. Get Into a Back-to-School Mindset With Advice From 12 Youth Soccer Coaches

Start the school year off on the right foot with insights from coaches who understand how the game translates to life off the field.

Late summer is always the hardest on parents. The pool days are numbered. The long evenings are shortening. The school year is coming, and it doesn’t care how ready you are.

The back-to-school transition is never the clean handoff the calendar makes it look like. Every August, we tell ourselves this year will be different. You’ll get ahead of it. Lunch prep sorted by Sunday. Bedtime routine locked in a week early. Screen-time rules clearly communicated and actually enforced. You’ll draw up this plan with the kind of granular, paranoid attention to detail that Guardiola brings to a cup final. But then, it’s all a disaster by Tuesday.

If you’re looking for an actual strategy that holds up, go to the park on a Saturday morning, find the sideline, and start listening to whoever is coaching.

These are people managing every extreme of human emotion — low blood sugar, wounded pride, full-on existential crises — all while trying to stop a five-way argument over who gets the neon green goalie pinnies. If they don’t know something useful, nobody does. So we hit up a dozen youth soccer coaches for their best back-to-school advice.

I tell my girls this on the first day of every season, and I mean it every time. Some days we’re doing your favorite thing. Some days we’re doing the thing you hate. The thing you hate is usually the thing that needs work. That’s not a coincidence. I don’t let them skip the hard drills because they don’t feel like it. I don’t let them drift to the stuff they’re already good at and call it practice. That’s not practice. That’s just playing around.

The subject your kid is dreading going back to — that’s the one. That’s the drill they need to run. Don’t negotiate them out of it. Make the deal: Do the work first, then we talk. It’s the same conversation I have at practice every Tuesday and Thursday, and it works there, too.

I don’t do big speeches. I never have. I’ve seen coaches do the whole thing — the whiteboard, the clipboard, the fire-and-brimstone season opener — and the kids are bored by the second sentence. So I just ask one question: What kind of teammate do you want? And they tell me. Funny. Helpful. Somebody who doesn’t make you feel bad when you mess up. Somebody who actually passes the ball. I write it all down. Then I say, good — now be all of that.

It’s not complicated. It’s just that nobody asks them the question directly and then holds them to the answer. Try it before school starts. Ask your kid what kind of friend they want to have this year. Then have the second half of that conversation.

I’ve been doing this since before most of these parents were driving their kids to practice, and the one thing that has never changed is this: Effort is the one thing every single kid controls completely. Talent, you’re born with, or you’re not. Height, same thing. But running back on defense when you’re tired? Picking yourself up after a bad touch and going again? That’s a choice. I’ve had kids with every physical tool in the world coast through and wonder why they weren’t improving. I’ve had kids who couldn’t trap a ball if their life depended on it go on to be captains because they simply refused to stop working.

Teachers see it the same way I do. The kid who stays after, asks questions, turns things in on time — that kid builds a reputation. And that reputation opens doors that talent alone doesn’t.

Every season, I get at least one kid who shows up on day one with opinions. Wants to play a different position, run a different shape, do things the way her last team did it. And look — I love that. I want players who think about the game. But there’s an order of operations. You don’t get to redesign a system you don’t understand yet. So the rule is: First month, you learn why we do what we do. Why we press from the front. Why we switch the point of attack the way we do.

Once you understand the why, then you’ve earned the right to push back.

A new school year means new teachers with their own ways of doing things. The kid who spends the first few weeks actually paying attention — figuring out how this classroom works before deciding what they think of it — that kid is so far ahead of the one who comes in with their arms already crossed.

I have a rule on this team, and it has been the same rule since my first season: You get three seconds after a mistake. Three seconds to be upset, to be frustrated, to feel whatever you feel. Then your head comes back up, and you get back in position. Because here’s the thing: The play is still happening. The game didn’t stop because you had a bad touch. And if you’re standing there feeling sorry for yourself, you’re now two mistakes deep instead of one.

I tell parents this, too, because it applies to everything. Your kid is going to fail a test this year. They’re going to say something wrong in class and feel embarrassed about it. They’re going to have a bad day. In life situations off the field, you get more than three seconds, but the same lesson applies. Acknowledge the mistake and then head up, back in position. The recovery is the name of the game.

I am obsessive about communication on the field. Obsessive. Not yelling, not blaming — information. Constant, useful, real-time information between players. Where you are, what you see, what they should do next. Most kids go completely silent under pressure, and that is exactly backwards from what you need. When it’s hardest to talk is when talking matters most.

I tell my players: A quiet team is a confused team. And a confused team gives the ball away. It’s the same thing off the field. The kid who speaks up in class, who says hi to the kid sitting alone at lunch, who tells a friend when something’s wrong — that kid ends up in the middle of things. The good things. Make some noise this year. Say something.

I played college soccer, and I will tell you that the thing nobody taught me until it was almost too late was how to rest. We were all conditioned to think that more was always better — more sprints, more film, more time in the gym. And there’s a point where more just breaks you. The best thing I ever did for my game was learn to take recovery seriously. Sleep. Real sleep. Not optional, not a treat — part of the program.

I build rest into my players’ weeks now, and I don’t let them feel guilty about it. The brain works the same way the body does. It consolidates everything it learned while you sleep. So if your kid is heading back to school and you’re letting them stay up until midnight on their phone — that’s not a small thing. That’s undermining everything they did that day. Rest is not laziness. I promise you it’s not.

I’ve been watching kids show up to this field for a long time, and I can tell you — the ones who get there early are different. Not because they’re more talented. Because they’ve had time to settle in. They’ve already touched a ball, already talked to a teammate, already figured out where they are and what they’re doing before anything’s officially started. They’re comfortable. The ones sprinting in right at the whistle are always the ones who take the whole first half to find their rhythm.

So on the first day of school, get there early. Your kid will have the chance to find the right classroom, ask any questions, and breathe a little bit. It’s a small thing that changes the whole morning.

I coach little kids. Eight-year-olds. So I see a lot of feelings on this field, and I’ve been real clear about my policy since day one: All the feelings are allowed. You can cry. You can tell me you need a minute. You can be upset. None of that is a problem. What you cannot do is walk off this field and decide you’re done. That’s the one thing I won’t accept. And I don’t say it mean — I just say it clearly, and I say it early, so it’s already been said when the moment comes.

Back to school is hard for a lot of kids, and I think parents sometimes feel like they’re supposed to pretend it isn’t. The anxiety is real. The overwhelm is real. Your kid can feel all of it and still go. That’s actually the lesson — that you’re allowed to struggle and still show up. Those two things can both be true at the same time.

I think about the game the way I think about conversation. There are moments when you have to speak — when you see the opening, and you have to take it, because if you wait, it’ll be gone. And there are moments when the best thing you can do is find the person in a better position and give it to them. The hardest thing to coach is the judgment between those two moments. A player who always shoots is a ball hog. A player who always passes is invisible. The great ones — the really great ones — know the difference in real time.

That’s an ego conversation as much as it’s a soccer conversation. Knowing when to speak up in class and when to let someone else take the floor. When to lead a group project and when to step back and support. It’s one of the harder things to teach, and one of the more important ones. Start having that conversation now, before the year starts.

I want my players to come to me. That’s the whole thing. I make myself as available as I possibly can because I know from experience that the kids who ask questions are the ones who get better. Not always the most talented kids — just the ones who seek feedback and then actually do something with it. Every season, the gap I notice most isn’t about skill. It’s about which kids advocate for themselves and which ones wait to be noticed.

Teachers work the same way I do. They want to help — they really do — but they’re managing a roomful of kids, and they can’t chase all of them down. The ones who stay after, send the email, ask what they missed and what they can do better — those are the ones who get more of the good stuff. It’s not about being the favorite. It’s about knowing how to ask for help. That skill will serve your kid for the rest of their life.

I coach at the level where it starts to get serious. Parents are thinking about high school rosters, kids are thinking about highlight reels, everybody’s tracking individual stats. And I am here to tell you — from where I stand on this sideline — that the players who make the biggest difference are almost never the ones you’d expect.

I’ve had physically gifted kids who played every game like it was an audition and made everyone around them worse for it. And I’ve had kids who, by every measurable standard, were average, who won us games because they made their teammates better. They covered for people, they communicated, and they did the stuff that doesn’t show up in the box score.

We spend so much time on our kids as individuals — their grades, their performance, their future — that we sometimes forget to teach them how to be good at being part of something. That’s a skill too. Maybe the most important one. The school year is long and almost entirely a team sport. Remind them.

#8139. 46 Gifts For Tweens & Teens That Won't Get An Eye-Roll (Probably)

Here are the gifts that’ll actually pass the vibe check.

Buying gifts for tweens and teens can be a special kind of holiday torture. Don’t get us wrong; it’s so much fun when you get it right. But it doesn’t always go that way, largely because their likes and wants are a moving target. Last year they wanted everything from the toy aisle. Now they want... a hoodie? A lip balm that ~everyone~ has? “Just money”? And boy, if you get it wrong, they’ll let you know. (It’s in the eyes.)

Since many of us on the Scary Mommy team are living with these outspoken arbiters of taste, we’ve done the reconnaissance for you. Some of these gifts are cozy staples they’ll wear on repeat until spring, like ultra-soft sweats. Some are creative outlets that aren’t too “kiddish,” like a retro digital camera. And some are the niche little things they’ll be weirdly thrilled to find in their stocking, like cloud-shaped body mists.

Basically, it’s a big ol’ list of things they’ll love... even if they’d never admit it out loud.

This is exactly the kind of open-ended, screen-free creative experience that I actually feel good putting under the tree. The Charmspring Create Kit Enchanted is developed by childhood experts and designed to spark genuine imagination and independent play, which means I hand it over to my daughter and she disappears into her own world for a very satisfying amount of time. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social

I got these for my athlete nephew, who had previously informed me that Bruce Bolt is THE BEST brand, full stop. I’ll admit I checked them out when they arrived, and I was seriously impressed by the quality. They feel incredible, look super cool (this electric-pink-aqua-blue combo was my nephew’s top pick), and the super-grippy palm is designed for confident catches. He’s worn these — along with the tackified compression arm sleeves — to his games this season, and swears they’re magic. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

These cloud-shaped body mists are cute enough to be a bag charm (trending) but durable enough to stand up to the wear and tear of living on a middle schooler's backpack. The scents are just right for the tween and teen age group too — not too childish, but not too mature either. I gave two of them to my 13-year-old niece, who used them up, and I love them as a stocking stuffer idea! — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

In the summer, the teens wear their Birkenstocks, and in the winter they switch to their UGGs — it is just the way of the world. I have declared these shoes too expensive to purchase as regular school clothes, so my daughter has appealed to Santa for help. He obliges. And since my kids also refuse to wear coats all winter, I'm happy to at least get them in some shoes that have a fuzzy lining. And for purchasing, I can't say it enough: Always go through Zappos so you can exchange and return things while dealing with the best customer service ever. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social

The Huffy GRM is exactly the kind of big holiday gift that makes a kid absolutely lose it on Christmas morning! The 24-inch frame is perfect for older kids ready to upgrade from their first bike, and the GRM has a sleek, sporty look that feels genuinely cool rather than obviously like a kids’ bike. It comes mostly assembled right out of the box so the Christmas morning setup is not a three-hour ordeal, and Huffy has been making reliable, fun bikes for decades at a price point that makes a big gift actually achievable. — Katie Garrity

My 15-year-old and I are both big Grace & Stella fans, so we were pumped to try these new Luscious Lip Gloss Butters. They did not disappoint! They glide on smooth and dewy, not sticky, and they smell amazing too. My favorite detail is the little keychain attachment, so my daughter can clip it to her backpack or keys and always have it on hand (read: stop “borrowing” mine). These would make a great stocking stuffer for any tween or teen. — Julie Sprankles

Seriously, how cute is this? My tween with long, straight hair is ready for her own arsenal of haircare products, and I desperately need her to stop stealing stuff from my bathroom, including my hair dryer. I love how fun this is, I love the accessories, and I love how it's affordable but from a really trusted haircare brand. We went with the pink. — Sarah Aswell

For the tween or teen on your list who could use a little support in the self-care and mental wellness department, a Therabox subscription is one of the most thoughtful gifts you can give. Each monthly box is curated by licensed therapists and packed with full-size wellness and self-care products designed to support emotional health, reduce stress, and encourage healthy habits. It arrives like a gift every single month, which makes it the present that keeps going long after the holidays are over, and the therapist-curated angle means every product inside actually has a purpose beyond just smelling nice. It’s a gift that says “I see you and I want you to feel good” in the most tangible way possible! — Katie Garrity

I have two tweens who are total musicheads, so I knew they’d flip for this Marshall Emberton III portable speaker. It’s a total upgrade from tinny phone audio, with that classic, cool Marshall look and full 360-degree sound. As a mom, I really appreciate that it’s built to handle real life: dustproof, waterproof, and the battery lasts 32+ hours on a single charge. — Julie Sprankles

Practically every child I know is into some form of lip balm, which is great because personally I didn't discover it until much later in life and now adore it, too. These lip balms make a great stocking stuffer: they're cute, they smell awesome (they come in kid-friendly flavors like "Frosted Sugar Plum" and "Candy Cane Fluff), and they're affordable. Add to cart stat. — Kate Auletta

Sometimes my teen's Christmas list just looks like a list of hoodies. One of her all-time favorites is this new classic from Hollister. These are super soft and oversized (but not huge), making it easily fall into the "my favorite hoodie" territory. I also bought these for my boy nephews for the holidays — you just really can't go wrong with these, I swear. — Sarah Aswell

This sleep set has completely changed our bedtime routine. The Dreamjellie pillow is designed specifically for kids and teens, with a shape that supports proper alignment whether they sleep on their side, back, or stomach, and the whole set comes with everything needed for a genuinely cozy, sleep-optimized setup. Getting a tween to actually wind down and sleep well is one of the great challenges of this age, and having bedding that feels special and is actually designed for their bodies makes a real difference. — Katie Garrity

This might be the gift that gets the biggest reaction from my gamer teen this year! It snaps right onto their phone and turns it into a handheld gaming console, with full-size joysticks and rear buttons, plus a comfy ergonomic grip. It works with almost any game that supports controllers, from Roblox and Minecraft to Xbox and PlayStation remote play. They can even go wireless and play on a tablet, PC, or TV! My husband fully looks forward to helping my son “test” this out when it comes in. — Julie Sprankles

I have a feeling many tween girls in my life will live for this gift: It’s a locket and strawberry-scented lipgloss in one. The lip gloss is cruelty-free, nut-free, and gluten-free, and is gentle enough for little kids to use over and over again. I also love that, once the gloss is gone, a message reading “You Are Super!” appears. I couldn’t love this more. — Kate Auletta

This is a new brand for me, but they have so many cute, affordable clothes that really seem to speak to my two teen kids. This double-layered shirt creates such a cool look (SO reminiscent of 90s Delia's, by the way), and it doesn't break the bank. I feel like I can buy a few cute shirts from here and make my kid's whole month. — Sarah Aswell

For the tween or teen who is living on their phone camera but deserves something that actually feels like a real creative tool, the Lola is the answer. The silver color is genuinely stunning and the kind of thing a style-conscious tween will want to carry everywhere and photograph everything with. — Katie Garrity

Both of my teens love to create fun little skits and videos as a creative outlet, so I figured it was time to get them an actual tripod instead of watching them precariously balance their phones on random objects to get the shot. I like that this one extends up to 71 inches, and that the Bluetooth works from up to 33 feet away. Plus, it folds down to 13 inches and weighs about a pound, making it easy to toss in a backpack. Oh, and it’s super affordable! — Julie Sprankles

I’m sort of like a tween in that I, too, live for a ridiculously fun bag. What I love about this is that you can position the bear (it also comes as a panda, unicorn, and fuzzy heart) to look like it's hugging you. It’s completely adorable and makes a great gift for tweens everywhere. — Kate Auletta

My 11-year-old is an art fanatic, but finding the right kits for her can be hard, as a lot of stuff is a little too "kidish." But she loves these eraser kits by Pretty Pixel, which allow her to either use templates or create her own characters. She loves making erasers for friends or challenging herself to make her favorite anime characters. One thing I love? The kits to buy more eraser materials are super affordable. — Sarah Aswell

For the Swiftie on your list who has everything, this is the gift that genuinely surprises them. Historic Newspapers compiles real newspaper coverage of Taylor Swift’s career from her earliest days all the way through her record-breaking eras, printed and bound into a beautiful keepsake book that reads like a time capsule of pop culture history. It is the kind of deeply personal, one-of-a-kind gift that no amount of merch shopping replicates, and for a tween or teen who has grown up watching Taylor dominate the world, seeing it all documented in real news print is going to hit differently. — Katie Garrity

If your teen’s bedroom doubles as a gaming den (hi, my son), let me put you on these Nanoleaf Blocks! They combine customizable smart lighting with shelves and pegboards so your gamer can mix and build a custom wall feature around their PC. They also connect with other Nanoleaf products, so the system can grow with them. But the reactive lighting is the real showstopper: When my son plays a game, the blocks’ lighting shifts to match the colors on his screen, creating a super-cool immersive experience. — Julie Sprankles

I'm a fan of anything that gets my kids off screens, and this Camp Snap Mini Camcorder did not come to play. It's compact, it's screen-free, and it has point-and-shoot recording (just like the old days!) with five film-inspired filters. There's no playback screen, no Wi-Fi, and no apps required — what a welcome change, huh? Definitely getting this for my older kid for Christmas. — Kate Auletta

This brand, SMOKO, has so many cute things that both of my teens would gladly die for. But this couch potato drinking a boba tea? That lets you turn off the overhead lights that my children hate with their whole hearts? Priceless. These are at a great price point, too, for things like friends' birthday gifts. — Sarah Aswell

Cloud Nine’s sweatpants have a reputation that genuinely precedes them. The fabric is that buttery, weightless softness kids refuse to take off once they put them on, and for a tween with strong opinions about comfort, this is basically a guaranteed win. They are the kind of cozy, elevated loungewear that looks cute enough to wear out but feels good enough to sleep in, which at this age is basically the holy grail of getting dressed. — Katie Garrity

These I Love Aromie Bakery plushies are adorable and smell SO good. Snuggymug is a cuddly little hot cocoa puppy, and when you squeeze his ear, his cheeks light up and he releases a visible puff of chocolate-scented mist. (Yes, really... it’s magical.) It’s a super-fun sensory gift that’s equal parts cuddle buddy and collectible. There are six characters, and I have no doubt my teens will not rest until they have all of them! — Julie Sprankles

My kids are sadly growing out of the matching family pajama era — it's just too babyish for them. But luckily for me, there are some more teen-friendly options out there that work for everyone. I LOVE these Sunshine Society silky jammies that feel amazing and also have a really fun print that even the most eye-rolling teen will accept into their lives. — Sarah Aswell

If your tween goes through hair ties like they’re disappearing into a black hole, this set is a lifesaver because it comes with 36 clips, bands, and barrettes in a bright mix of colors. It all lives in its own organizer case, which means her accessories finally have a home that isn’t the bottom of a backpack or your car’s cup holder. At $12, it’s the kind of stocking stuffer or small gift she’ll actually use every single day! — Katie Garrity

I got these CMF Clip Pro earbuds for my teen, who immediately fell in love with the coral colorway. (It’s so pretty!) They have an open-ear clip design, so instead of jamming buds into her ears, they hug the outside of the ear. This makes them (a) stay put and (b) actually comfortable to wear. The sound is really fantastic, too, with hi-res audio and clear voice technology for calls. — Julie Sprankles

My daughter informs me that these hoodies are THE COOLEST. Hoodies that can be layered and hoodies with buttons instead of ties are in, and this has both. And, more importantly to me, Athleta has really nice quality clothes that are nowhere near as expensive as some of the other athleisure brands my daughter yearns for. I got this one on sale for under $30! — Sarah Aswell

Buying this for my daughter because it combines two things she’s obsessed with, Squishmallows and anything that’s satisfying to squeeze, into one tiny, glittery package. It’s filled with slow-flow glitter and has a shape-memory design, so no matter how hard she stretches and squishes it, it bounces right back into its Squishmallows shape. At under $10, it’s a great stocking stuffer for any tween who needs something to do with her hands (and honestly, a few moms I know too)! — Katie Garrity

These M2U NYC Makeup Blending Sponges are the cutest, most affordable stocking stuffers for tweens or teens who are into makeup. The collection includes four latex-free sponges, each with an adorable animal on its packaging: a rabbit, a panda, a fox, and a cat. Each “animal” does a different job, from precise contouring to blending around tricky spots like the nose and under-eyes. And at only $22 for all four, how could you not? — Julie Sprankles

The problem with tweens is that they say they don't want any toys for Christmas, but when the holiday rolls around and they only get clothes and skincare products, they realize they are sad (and that they are still children who want toys!) For my 11-year-old, the answer was this mini pottery wheel and spin art set. It is fun enough to feel like a toy, but it lets them create cool art and feels kind of just like art supplies. This is also a great birthday present for elementary-aged kids. — Sarah Aswell

For the parent who isn’t ready to hand over a smartphone but wants their kid to be reachable, the TickTalk 6 is the middle ground, because it does calls, video calls, real texts, and GPS with zero games, social media, or open internet. You decide who’s on the approved contact list from the app, your kid still gets SOS and 911 calling plus a walkie-talkie feature, and there’s nothing on the watch for her to get sucked into. It’s a big gift, but it’s the one that gives a tween a little independence while you keep the controls. — Katie Garrity

I recently discovered Fun Fact Co., and I’m obsessed with how the brand turns educational material into actual art. I have two teens with very different feelings about math: one loves numbers, and the other really struggles with them. This Multiplication Table Print appeals to both of them. It highlights prime, Fibonacci, and square numbers, which gives my math lover something extra to geek out over, while my other kid gets a handy, judgment-free reference tool. And it looks great on our study wall! — Julie Sprankles

All my tween daughters want for Christmas is sweatpants. And all I want for Christmas is to find some high-quality, AFFORDABLE sweatpants for my tweens. This pair from Pacsun fits the bill. They're only $35, they come in a rainbow of colors, and the style is really cute. They are "one size fits most," which was a little concerning, but I did find that they fit both my very petite 11-year-old and my athletic almost-14-year-old. So! — Sarah Aswell

For the tween or teen who treats her AirPods like a fashion accessory, a Burga case is the cool-girl upgrade that makes the boring white case look like part of her outfit. It comes in a ton of printed designs, gives the case 360° protection from drops and scratches, still works with wireless charging, and even lets the LED light show through. It also clips right onto a backpack or belt loop with the included carabiner, which means it’s a whole lot harder to lose and a whole lot more stylish to carry! — Katie Garrity

For years, I always forgot to get my kids presents they could use in the summer — but I'm not making that mistake anymore. I always get my kids a swimsuit and cover-up, and I always get them a game that's fun to play outside. This year, I got them Basa, which is a four-person paddle game that's easy to set up anywhere you have enough open space, from the grass to sand. I love that this has the feel of pickleball but you don't need to seek out a court, and that it's easy to start playing right away. — Sarah Aswell

I will admit this gift may be more for me than my teen, but still... I stand by the fact that it makes a great gift if, like me, you have a new driver in the house. This little treasure plugs right into their car’s diagnostic port and connects to a phone over Bluetooth, so if that dreaded “check engine” light pops on, my teen can see what’s wrong right away, along with verified repair suggestions. It’s a smart way to teach a new driver some basic car care, and I appreciate that it’s a one-time purchase with no subscription required. — Julie Sprankles

I don't want my kid to grow up without experiencing music the way I did: listening to entire albums, offline. And the cool part is that kids are discovering their parents' CD collections just like we discovered our parents' record collections. For under $100, Lola has released a rechargeable, portable CD player that comes with wired headphones included. The only real differences? This has a great anti-skip feature, and it can be charged via a USB port. Um, I kind of want one too? — Sarah Aswell

For the tween or teen who needs a break from holiday chaos, this winter-themed bath bomb is a little spa moment she can fizz away in, with a light blue and white design covered in an icy snowflake pattern. It melts into glistening blue water scented with eucalyptus, peppermint, and lemongrass oils for a cool, fresh, tingly bath that feels like a snow day without the cold. It’s made in Canada, arrives with no packaging, and it’s a perfect, easy stocking stuffer for any bath-loving kid on your list! — Katie Garrity

My artsy teen would take one of these coloring blankets in every single design if they could, and would happily gift one to each of their friends too. Each 50-by-60-inch blanket comes printed with an original design by a Minnesota-based artist, from galaxies to vintage florals, ready to color in. We have the under-the-sea version, and we’ve been totally nerding out over all the cool sea creatures to fill in. It’s such a fun, creative, cozy outlet that turns into a one-of-a-kind keepsake. Bonus: It’s from a woman-owned business! — Julie Sprankles

For the teen who’s into Pilates, barre, yoga, or just wants the cutest cozy socks, these grippy full-foot socks are a $16 stocking stuffer she’ll actually wear, in a pretty green with a little yellow “namaste” on them. They have a no-slip grip on the bottom, a cushioned terry footbed, compression arch support, and a padded ankle rest, all in soft, moisture-wicking cotton. They’re snug and supportive without feeling stiff, which makes them the perfect gift for the kid who is always stretching, sliding around the house, or heading to class. — Katie Garrity

This is my artsy daughter's BIG holiday present, and she is absolutely going to flip out. I have gotten her so many markers over the years, and these are her absolute favorites to work with. And as she's graduated from Crayola to more grown-up art needs, this company has been really great for us. I also love that this comes in a sturdy carrying case and with a swatch card, which my daughter loves to fill out as soon as she gets a new set. — Sarah Aswell

For the tween or teen who's obsessed with her dog (or everyone else's), this dog-themed earring set from Pip Pop Post is a super cute way to show it off. The earrings are made from hypoallergenic 18k gold-plated stainless steel with colorful enamel, and they're free of nickel, lead, and copper, so they're comfortable for sensitive ears. They use flat screw-back posts that stay put through sleep, sports, and school, and they're waterproof and sweat-proof, so she can wear them 24/7 without a second thought! — Katie Garrity

Every year, we get the kids a holiday-themed puzzle from Mudpuppy. The quality is great, and the puzzles are challenging without being a nightmare. Many of them have foil details, which make them so pretty and fun. Especially as my kids get older and there are fewer traditional toys under the tree, having a puzzle to settle around on Christmas afternoon while we watch 'Miracle on 34th Street 'is a real crowd-pleaser. — Sarah Aswell

If you were a kid in the ‘90s like I was, you probably remember the absolute thrill of a fresh pack of Gelly Roll pens. Well, I’m happy to report they’re still just as magical for tweens and teens today! This 74-pen gift set from Sakura has every color imaginable, from metallics to bright neons, and I know my artsy teen is going to flip when they find it under the tree. The pens are perfect for doodling, coloring, junk journaling, or even just making handmade cards for friends (one of my teen’s favorite hobbies). And, yes, I’ll obviously be borrowing a few for my own desk. — Julie Sprankles

#8135. Beautiful Eastern Orthodox Baby Names and Their Meanings

Timeless Eastern Orthodox baby names that celebrate heritage, culture, and tradition across generations

Have you ever wondered how a name can carry the weight of centuries?

When it comes to naming a baby, tradition often speaks louder than trends. For families connected to Eastern Orthodox heritage, names are more than labels. They’re echoes of centuries of culture, history, and community. These names have been passed down through generations, carrying stories of emperors, scholars, saints, and everyday people who shaped Orthodox life.

From the regal Constantine to the graceful Anastasia, this list of Eastern Orthodox baby names celebrates timeless choices that honor tradition while remaining beautiful and relevant today.

Names are more than words. They’re vessels of memory, culture, and continuity. Within Eastern Orthodox tradition, baby names reflect centuries of heritage, often inspired by Byzantine rulers, revered scholars, and beloved figures whose stories shaped communities across Greece, Russia, the Balkans, and beyond. Choosing an Orthodox baby name isn’t just about finding something elegant; it’s about honoring the past while giving your child a timeless identity that will carry meaning for generations.

From Greek Orthodox names that sparkle with classical charm to Slavic Orthodox names rooted in resilience, these choices embody tradition in its purest form. They remind us that while trends may fade, tradition endures, and a name chosen with care becomes a lasting gift.

Strong, dignified, and steeped in tradition, these boy names have been passed down through centuries of Orthodox heritage. They carry echoes of emperors, scholars, and timeless figures, making them enduring choices for families who value culture and continuity.

Aaron – Exalted, strong; St. Aaron the Priest

Abraham – Father of many; Patriarch of Israel

Achilles – Hero of the Greeks; symbol of courage

Adrian – From Hadria; St. Adrian the Martyr

Alexander – Defender of men; borne by saints and emperors

Alexios – Defender, helper; St. Alexios the Man of God

Anastasios – Resurrection; linked to Easter tradition

Anthony (Antonios) – Priceless one; St. Anthony the Great

Aristides – Best purpose; early Christian philosopher

Aristotle – Best purpose; classical Greek heritage

Arsenios – Virile, strong; St. Arsenios the Great

Athanasios – Immortal; St. Athanasius of Alexandria

Basil (Vasilios) – Royal, kingly; St. Basil the Great

Benjamin – Son of the right hand; biblical patriarch

Christos – Anointed one; direct reference to Christ

Christopher – Bearer of Christ; St. Christopher the Martyr

Constantine – Steadfast, constant; Emperor Constantine the Great

Cosmas (Kosmas) – Order, harmony; St. Kosmas of Aetolia

Damian – To tame, subdue; St. Damian the Martyr

Demetrios – Devoted to Demeter; St. Demetrios of Thessaloniki

Dimitri – Earth lover; Slavic Orthodox tradition

Dominic – Belonging to the Lord; Western Orthodox usage

#8134. I'm Not A "Bowel Normie" & I Still Have Three Healthy Kids

My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life.

I became sick when I was 12. It happened out of nowhere. We were on a family trip to New York City to celebrate New Year’s Eve in Times Square. I stood out on the Statue of Liberty’s crown, sipping the (extravagantly priced) hot chocolate my parents bought me to combat the cold, gazing in awe at the dazzling metropolis, and was suddenly overcome with nausea. That night, I began vomiting, running to the toilet, and developed a high fever. I couldn’t even make it to the window to see the ball drop.

Over the next three years, I spent much of my time in doctor’s offices and bathrooms, with bloating, constipation, diarrhea and bleeding. I was in pain, mostly searing pangs. Who knew when they would hit? I went for X-rays, scopes, breath tests, physical exams; I tried medications, carbon supplements, acupuncture. Steroids worked miraculously at first, then not at all. Experimental drugs went through me completely undigested. I began to evacuate the lining of my own colon; it looked like a thin white snake. My blood count was so low I was repeatedly hospitalized for blood transfusions and iron infusions. It appeared I had very severe ulcerative colitis.

During this time, I was in 7th to 10th grades, the time of first loves, frenemies, tattoos and drivers ed. But as someone with acute bowel disease, my teenage life was increasingly limited. Want a ride home? No thanks. I was worried that whoever was driving would take detours, keeping me away from a toilet. The metro was scary; what if it stalled and I was stuck? I went to school but sat next to the door of the classroom. It was hard for me to go to boy-girl get-togethers: I couldn’t even sit through a movie in someone’s basement, and what if the bathroom was within earshot? The logistics were so difficult, the risk of embarrassment too high. I stopped attending most things.

All teenagers deal with their body changing, with it being out of their control. My body was waging war on me, emitting shameful sounds, smells and sights without my consent. It felt like I, Little Judy, was buried somewhere deep inside this morass of sickly flesh, this thing that all these ancient doctors were probing, trying to decipher. Had I done something to cause this? Was it my fault? I didn’t not-love my body, I hated it.

When my friends were exploring sexuality, I recoiled. For one, it’s hard to think about smooching when you’re doubled down in anguish. Constantly exposed to the medical world, I’d created strong barriers, dissociating from my physical experience.

Not to mention, how could I possibly share what I was going through with anyone? My peers were worried about algebra tests; I was worried about blood tests. My friends gossiped about trying drugs; I was on more drugs than half the school combined! I went to doctors who mentioned the possibility of developing cancer. I felt misunderstood, alone, and so very ugly. I didn’t know how to let anyone get close.

By tenth grade, my life was completely in the toilet, literally. Surgery was offered as an option. Major surgery: they would remove my entire large intestine colon and create a pouch from part of the small intestine that would, hopefully, work as a de facto colon. Doctors kept postponing the procedure, worried about the risks. But I insisted on the operation. I told my parents, if they didn’t take me, I’d take the bus.

So, at 15, I had my entire colon removed. My pouch was amazing; I was not a “bowel normie,” and I couldn’t eat with abandon, but I lived a mostly pain-free life. I remained relatively healthy through my twenties, eventually dating (and making up for lost time!). I got married at age 31 to a man who I was able to open up to about my chronic condition, and who was willing to support my toilet paper habit. But then came the question: was my body robust enough to have a baby? Could I get past all my shame, all my corporeal disappointment, to create a life? And should I be a parent, i.e. would my children end up sick too? I wobbled for two years.

Then, the second I’d decided to maybe even consider trying to get pregnant, my gynecologist enrolled me in a fertility clinic, saying, “People with your surgeries have so much trouble, there’s not a minute to waste.” A few weeks later, I was doing bloodwork at my local clinic so they could send the results to the fertility center. Only, it turned out, as a squealing nurse revealed, I was already pregnant.

The nine months passed seamlessly, bowel-wise, except for some excruciating bouts of gas that had become trapped under my growing belly. My first daughter was born healthy via C-section (recommended, as natural childbirth carried a risk of damaging the pouch). Though I did have a dangerous and frightening ectopic pregnancy a few years later when trying for my second — most likely due to scar tissue from the old surgery — I ultimately ended up having three children which is a miracle, and also, a little insane. My body, once a disintegrating and diseased lump of organs, had made so much life! Never mind years of yoga and pilates, finally, I felt strong. And even, a little bit beautiful.

Judy Batalion is a New York Times bestselling author of award-winning nonfiction and fiction. Her essays have appeared in The New York Times, The Washington Post, and Vogue, among others. Judy has a BA in the History of Science from Harvard, a PhD from the University of London, and has worked as a museum curator and university lecturer. She lives in New York City with her husband and three children.

We might have a while to wait until the third season of Wednesday drops on Netflix, but there's a new 'it' flower doing the rounds that's serving some serious Addams-flavored energy... and people have fallen hard for its gothic energy.

This should come as little surprise to those on top of their gardening trends, of course, because much of 2026 has come with a distinctly gothic twist – whether that's due to the gothic romance of Wuthering Heights, the bewitching gardens seen in Practical Magic 2, or Kat Von D's maximalist approach to black tulips.

Still, it's nice to see something a little different steal the spotlight from the world of pastel blooms, right? And Lilium 'Nightrider', the nearly black lily that's set to appeal to anyone who prefers their flowers with a little more drama, does exactly that.

With its rich purple-black petals and subtle satin-like sheen, this striking lily looks almost completely black in certain light. It's an unusually dramatic color for a summer flower, giving it an almost otherworldly and deeply Wednesday-coded quality that's hard to ignore.

Of course, it's not just the color that makes 'Nightrider' so special, or the fact that its upward-facing blooms appear in clusters on tall stems, creating a striking focal point wherever it's planted.

No, it's the fact that you don't need to be an expert gardener to enjoy this showstopper. Like other garden lilies, 'Nightrider' is relatively easy to grow, making it a really good choice for gardeners who want maximum visual impact without an overly complicated planting scheme.

The trick is to do the opposite of what you'd do with Wednesday Addams herself: give it a suitable sunny or lightly shaded position. Then, top it off with well-drained soil, then sit back and wait for that striking show come summertime!

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Shop Gothic Blooms That Wednesday Would Love:

It goes without saying that this is a flower for those who love a little mystery, dramatic contrasts and planting that makes a statement, which is why you need to think hard about the flowers you pop it next to.

With that in mind, try pairing its almost-black blooms with silver foliage, deep burgundy flowers or soft white planting for a really striking combination that feels like something straight out of your favorite gothic romance.

Alternatively, leave it to do its Wednesday-style thing, and let it stand alone in a container where its unusual coloring can take all the attention. One thing is certain: if you're looking to introduce a little gothic glamor to your garden, this nearly black lily deserves a place on your radar.

I am confident in saying that a certain Miss Addams would absolutely approve.

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.
